summary: Bupivacaine is a long-acting amide-type local anesthetic used for local or regional anesthesia and analgesia in surgical, dental, diagnostic, therapeutic, and obstetric procedures. Only the 0.25% and 0.5% concentrations are indicated for obstetric anesthesia; the 0.75% concentration is contraindicated in obstetric (paracervical and other obstetric) anesthesia because of reports of cardiac arrest with difficult resuscitation. Inadvertent intravascular injection or excessive plasma levels can cause local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) with CNS and cardiovascular effects; bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is notably more refractory to resuscitation than other local anesthetics. Use incremental dosing, the lowest effective dose, and frequent aspiration.
indications: Production of local or regional anesthesia or analgesia for surgery
Obstetrical procedures (only the 0.25% and 0.5% concentrations for obstetric anesthesia)

dosage.r: Local infiltration / nerve block / caudal / epidural
dosage.d: Most experience with single doses up to 175 mg without epinephrine and up to 225 mg with epinephrine 1:200,000
dosage.t: May repeat up to once every 3 hours
dosage.n: Use smallest dose/concentration for the desired effect; total daily dose should not exceed 400 mg in 24 hours

dosage.d: Administer in incremental doses of 3 to 5 mL
dosage.n: Allows detection of unintentional intravascular or intrathecal injection; 0.75% is for non-obstetric use only

dosage.d: Only 0.25% and 0.5% concentrations; 0.5% in 3 to 5 mL increments not exceeding 50 to 100 mg at any dosing interval
dosage.n: Precede repeat doses with an epinephrine-containing test dose if not contraindicated; 0.75% must NOT be used in obstetrics

dosage.d: Average 1.8 mL (9 mg) per injection site; an occasional second 1.8 mL (9 mg) dose if needed
dosage.n: Total per dental sitting should not ordinarily exceed 90 mg in a healthy adult; inject slowly with frequent aspiration
Reduce dose; elderly may reach higher peak plasma levels and have decreased clearance

admin: For parenteral use only; not for spinal anesthesia and not for intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier Block)
Avoid rapid injection of large volumes; use fractional (incremental) doses when feasible
Aspirate before and during injection to detect inadvertent intravascular or intrathecal placement
Use only single-dose ampules/vials (preservative-free) for caudal or epidural anesthesia; multiple-dose vials contain preservative
Inspect for particulate matter and discoloration; do not use if discolored, pinkish, darker than slightly yellow, or containing precipitate
Have resuscitation equipment, oxygen, and lipid emulsion immediately available before administration
moa: Bupivacaine is an amide-type local anesthetic that blocks the generation and conduction of nerve impulses by increasing the threshold for electrical excitation, slowing impulse propagation, and reducing the rate of rise of the action potential, presumably through inhibition of voltage-gated sodium channels. Clinically, nerve functions are lost in the order: pain, temperature, touch, proprioception, then skeletal muscle tone.

absolute: Obstetrical paracervical block anesthesia (has resulted in fetal bradycardia and death)
The 0.75% concentration is CONTRAINDICATED in obstetric anesthesia (associated with cardiac arrest and difficult resuscitation)
Known hypersensitivity to bupivacaine, to any amide-type local anesthetic, or to other components of the solution
relative: Not recommended for intravenous regional anesthesia (Bier Block)
Not approved for intra-articular infusion (reports of chondrolysis)
Severe hepatic disease (increased susceptibility to toxicity)
Elderly/debilitated and patients with cardiac disease (reduce dose)
Patients at risk for methemoglobinemia (e.g., G6PD deficiency, infants <6 months, concurrent oxidizing agents)
Sulfite sensitivity if using epinephrine-containing solutions (contain sodium metabisulfite)
Not recommended in pediatric patients younger than 12 years
monitor: Cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs and patient consciousness after each injection
Early signs of CNS toxicity (restlessness, anxiety, tinnitus, perioral numbness, tremors) and cardiovascular toxicity
Blood pressure for hypotension, especially patients over 65 with hypertension
Signs of methemoglobinemia (cyanosis, abnormal blood coloration)

preg: Used in obstetrics, but only the 0.25% and 0.5% concentrations are indicated for obstetric anesthesia; the 0.75% concentration is contraindicated in obstetric anesthesia. Bupivacaine is contraindicated for obstetrical paracervical block (fetal bradycardia and death reported). Bupivacaine has high (95%) plasma protein binding and a low fetal/maternal ratio (0.2 to 0.4). During treatment of systemic toxicity, maternal hypotension, or fetal bradycardia after regional block, keep the parturient in the left lateral decubitus position or manually displace the uterus to avoid aortocaval compression.
lact: Local anesthetics cross the placenta by passive diffusion and may be present in milk; bupivacaine has a low fetal/maternal ratio due to high protein binding. Data on use during breastfeeding are limited; weigh clinical need against potential infant exposure.
renal: The kidney is the main excretory organ for local anesthetics and their metabolites (only ~6% of bupivacaine is excreted unchanged in urine). Renal disease and factors affecting urinary pH/perfusion can alter pharmacokinetics; use with caution.
hepatic: Amide local anesthetics are metabolized primarily in the liver via conjugation with glucuronic acid (major metabolite pipecoloxylidine). Patients with hepatic disease, especially severe disease, may be more susceptible to toxicity; reduce the dose.

major: Other local anesthetics or agents structurally related to amide local anesthetics - additive systemic toxicity
Drugs/conditions causing methemoglobinemia (e.g., other oxidizing agents) - increased methemoglobinemia risk
moderate: Drugs competing for plasma protein binding or causing acidosis - may diminish individual tolerance
Vasopressors and ergot-type oxytocics with epinephrine-containing solutions - risk of severe, persistent hypertension
interactions.alcohol: Not applicable for single-procedure parenteral use.
interactions.diagnostics: Toxic plasma levels depress cardiac conduction and excitability (AV block, ventricular arrhythmias on ECG); monitor for methemoglobinemia (cyanosis, abnormal blood color).

common: Hypotension (especially with epidural/spinal block and in patients over 65)
serious: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) - CNS excitation/depression progressing to convulsions, then respiratory arrest
Cardiovascular toxicity - myocardial depression, heart block, ventricular arrhythmias, cardiac arrest
Total or high spinal (apnea, hypotension, loss of consciousness) after unintended subarachnoid injection
Methemoglobinemia (may progress to seizures, arrhythmias, coma)
Persistent neurologic deficits, urinary/fecal incontinence, sphincter dysfunction after neuraxial block
rare: Allergic / anaphylactoid reactions (urticaria, angioedema including laryngeal edema, severe hypotension)
Chondrolysis after intra-articular infusion (not an approved use)
Cranial nerve palsies from cerebrospinal fluid loss
emergency: Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity (LAST): CNS toxicity (perioral numbness, tinnitus, agitation, seizures) and cardiovascular toxicity (arrhythmias, hypotension, cardiac arrest) from unintended intravascular injection or excessive plasma levels
Management: stop injection, secure airway, ventilate with 100% oxygen, control seizures, and give IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) plus supportive cardiopulmonary resuscitation
Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is more refractory to resuscitation than other local anesthetics - prolonged resuscitative efforts may be required
Methemoglobinemia: treat with methylene blue, oxygen, and supportive care after discontinuing oxidizing agents

monitoring: Continuous cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs and level of consciousness after each injection
Early symptoms of LAST (perioral/tongue numbness, tinnitus, lightheadedness, agitation) and progression to seizures or cardiovascular collapse
Blood pressure and heart rate for hypotension and bradycardia, particularly in elderly/hypertensive patients
Signs of high or total spinal block (respiratory compromise, hypotension)
Cyanosis or abnormal blood color suggesting methemoglobinemia
counsel: This medicine is given by a trained clinician during a procedure
Report immediately any ringing in the ears, numbness around the mouth or tongue, metallic taste, dizziness, restlessness, or palpitations during or after injection
Temporary numbness, weakness, or loss of sensation in the anesthetized area is expected and will resolve
Tell the clinician about any prior reaction to local anesthetics, asthma/sulfite sensitivity, heart or liver disease, or if pregnant
Avoid injury to the numb area (e.g., biting cheek/tongue after dental anesthesia) until sensation returns
pk: Rapid; following dental injection usually 2 to 10 minutes
Peak blood levels after caudal/epidural/peripheral block in 30 to 45 minutes
About 2.7 hours in adults; 8.1 hours in neonates
Long-acting; up to ~7 hours after dental use; prolonged by added epinephrine
Store at 20 to 25 C (68 to 77 F); protect epinephrine-containing solutions from light; discard if discolored or precipitated
pearls: The 0.75% concentration is contraindicated in obstetric anesthesia due to reports of maternal cardiac arrest with difficult resuscitation; use only 0.25% or 0.5% in obstetrics

LAST (Local Anesthetic Systemic Toxicity): suspect with CNS signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, seizures) and cardiovascular collapse - treat with IV lipid emulsion (Intralipid) plus airway, oxygen, and supportive resuscitation
Bupivacaine cardiotoxicity is more refractory to resuscitation than other local anesthetics and may require prolonged efforts
Use incremental 3 to 5 mL dosing with aspiration during epidural administration to detect intravascular or intrathecal placement
Contraindicated for obstetrical paracervical block (fetal bradycardia and death); not for IV regional (Bier) block or intra-articular infusion
Reduce dose in the elderly, debilitated, and those with cardiac or severe hepatic disease
missed: Not applicable - bupivacaine is administered as single or incremental doses by a clinician during a procedure rather than on a self-administered schedule.
overdose: Acute emergencies result from high plasma levels (overdose, rapid absorption, or unintended intravascular/subarachnoid injection) and manifest as local anesthetic systemic toxicity: CNS excitation (restlessness, tinnitus, tremors) progressing to convulsions, then depression, respiratory arrest, and cardiovascular collapse (myocardial depression, arrhythmias, cardiac arrest). Management: stop the drug, establish a patent airway, ventilate with 100% oxygen, control convulsions (e.g., benzodiazepine), support circulation with IV fluids and a vasopressor (ephedrine/epinephrine) as needed, and give IV lipid emulsion. Bupivacaine-induced cardiac arrest may require prolonged resuscitation. Keep pregnant patients in the left lateral decubitus position to avoid aortocaval compression. Contact Poison Help (1-800-222-1222).
